summary:
Novgorod Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and no oblast-level deviation from that framework has been sourced. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025), which sets the reference framework for this division, contains no division-specific information beyond the national position, and the Human Rights Watch reporting used to calibrate enforcement carries no Novgorod-specific figures. The oblast is assessed at the national score.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia. Same-sex marriage is prohibited and legal gender recognition is unavailable, so a trans visitor cannot obtain corrected identity documents or a marriage-based partner status in Novgorod Oblast. Gender reassignment surgery and legal changes of gender on official documents were banned outright in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year; the UK Home Office note records gender transition as banned under the national framework.

The Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023. The expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that promotes non-traditional sexual relations and, explicitly, anything justifying gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings, including the US State Department's Level 4 Do Not Travel advisory, carry explicit cautions directed at LGBT travellers.

Enforcement volume is documented. The UK Home Office records that at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024, with "gay propaganda" fines reaching 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) and 15 days' detention for individuals. Human Rights Watch reported 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols as of 30 June 2025, with sentences of up to 12 years' imprisonment, alongside 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, most of them on social media. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The tempo of the post-designation crackdown is established in the record. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over two years. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation.

Detention carries lethal risk. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

On protection machinery, the UK Home Office country policy and information note (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Physical coercion against transgender people is documented at national scale. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The case arose in Siberia, not in Novgorod Oblast, and is cited here as evidence of the coercive practices available within the national framework.

The extremist designation has produced liability for symbols rather than conduct alone: the article 20.3 cases recorded by Human Rights Watch concern display of banned symbols, mostly in social media posts, which means conduct with no physical presence in any particular oblast can still generate prosecution. Visitors and residents in Novgorod Oblast are exposed to the same online-monitoring risk as elsewhere in the country.

Raids and mass searches documented after the November 2023 ruling were concentrated in Moscow and St Petersburg, the country's two largest cities. No comparable operation in Novgorod Oblast has been sourced, and the absence of such reporting should not be read as evidence of a permissive local environment, since the oblast is scored on the national framework that governs policing there.

Official foreign government warnings place Russia at the highest travel-advisory tier with LGBT-specific cautions, which differs from the treatment of most destinations covered on this map and signals that the risk assessment is not a general-crime judgement.
localsOnly:
Residents of Novgorod Oblast cannot change the gender marker on Russian identity documents or undertake legal gender recognition, since the 2023 statute prohibits both gender reassignment surgery and legal changes of gender on official documents. Trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since the same year, so hormone therapy and surgical care cannot be obtained lawfully within the country.

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples under the national Constitution, so partners of oblast residents have no marital status, next-of-kin standing or associated residence rights derived from a relationship.

Residents face the same penalties recorded nationally: fines up to 400,000 rubles for propaganda offences, administrative conviction under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, and extremism charges carrying up to 12 years' imprisonment for participation in or display of symbols of the designated movement. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement across the country.

The UK Home Office treats LGBT+ people in Russia as members of a particular social group under the refugee convention, which governs UK asylum determinations involving oblast residents who leave the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether police in Novgorod Oblast have conducted raids, extremism prosecutions or administrative cases under article 20.3 since the November 2023 designation is not sourced. The Human Rights Watch figures are national totals with no regional breakdown, and no oblast-level enforcement data has been located.

Access to trans-affirming care, informal hormone supply networks and the operation of any local support or shelter organisations in Novgorod Oblast are not covered by the inventory and remain unresolved.

The UK Home Office note carries a June 2025 content date with a page update recorded on 12 August 2026; whether its description of the national framework has been revised since publication is not established here.

The conversion-therapy case documented by BBC Russian occurred near Novosibirsk and does not evidence conditions inside Novgorod Oblast.

Nothing in the inventory addresses border or entry screening practice at Novgorod Oblast crossing points, including whether identity documents are inspected for gender markers.
